title: Indexing & .at()
description: Arrays are zero-indexed; use .at() for ergonomic negative indexing from the end.

notes: arr[-1] does NOT give the last element — it returns undefined (negative is a string key, not an index).
Out-of-bounds access returns undefined silently — guard or use ?? for defaults.
.at() is ES2022; safe in modern browsers and Node 16+. Prefer it over arr[arr.length - 1].

questions.explain: `-1` isn't an index — it becomes the string key `"-1"`, which the array doesn't have, so the read is `undefined` rather than an error. `arr.at(-1)` is the form that counts from the end.
`.at()` accepts negatives and counts back from the end, so `-1` is the last element — the clean replacement for `arr[arr.length - 1]`.
Out-of-bounds reads are silent in JS — a missing index is just a missing key, so you get `undefined`, never a `RangeError`. Guard with `??` when you need a default.

options: getter that runs a count loop
questions.explain: `length` is a plain data property — `arr.length()` throws. It's also writable, not constant: `arr.length = 1` truncates `[1,2,3]` to `[1]` in place.

exercises.prompt: Log the first and last element using bracket indexing.
Two equivalent ways to read the LAST element — `.at(-1)` and the verbose bracket form. Blanks force you to type both.
